Woman punched and kicked for helping cousin move out

A woman who helped her cousin retrieve her belongings from an apartment after a fractious end to a relationship was punched in the face

The victim said her sleep has been disrupted and she cannot return to work since the attack

Monday, July 20, 2020 - 18:04 PM

Liam Heylin

A woman who helped her cousin in retrieving her belongings from an apartment after a fractious end to a relationship ended up being punched in the face and kneed or kicked in the ribs by the man.

Judge Olann Kelleher said he was concerned to read the victim impact statement, saying: "He threatened her: 'The people from Dublin will be down to take you out.' He then tried to get her to drop the charges."

Defence solicitor Frank Buttimer stressed that the case against 46-year-old Aran Green, of 6 Elderwood Park, Cork, went back a year and there was absolutely no question of any such threat being carried out or any contact of any kind being made by the defendant with the injured party.

Green pleaded guilty to a charge of assault causing harm to the woman, who was merely assisting her cousin.

Mr Buttimer said the accused had gathered €5,000 compensation for the woman, which he handed over at Cork District Court.

Judge Kelleher said it was a vicious attack and he noted from a victim impact report that her sleep had been completely disrupted in the year since and she had been unable to return to work.

Judge Kelleher said he would not finalise the case yesterday and wanted to make sure there would be no more trouble from the defendant. He adjourned sentencing until October 19.

Sergeant Davis said that, on August 18, 2019, the defendant's ex-girlfriend went to the apartment at Boreenmanna Road to retrieve clothing and other belongings. Mr Buttimer said the relationship had ended in a fractious manner.

Sgt Davis said the defendant's ex-girlfriend was accompanied by her cousin and they noticed her belongings strewn around outside the property.

Sgt Davis said the defendant arrived and assaulted the young woman with his ex-girlfriend, "grabbed her by the hair, punched her face and head and then kicked or kneed her in the ribs".

Mr Buttimer said the defendant only realised what he had done when investigating gardaí showed him CCTV.

"He is beyond remorseful for his actions," he said. "He has written a letter of apology."

Reference:
I leaned closer and saw a little discoloration near the hem of her dress. It was brown, sort of, but not like dirt. Like dried blood. Just beside it the fabric was torn.

"It struck a chord in me," she said and released hold of the dress. "Made me feel... funny. Like remembering something you thought you'd never think of again. I remembered crashing on a bicycle when I was a little girl, and I hurt my knee. This is blood."

"So you're wearing a dress from your childhood?"

"It appears so."

"You can recall a biking accident but not your name?"

"I guess seeing it is why I remembered it. You don't happen to know where we can find water, do you? I'm really thirsty."

"As am I. No, I'm sorry. I'm also sorry for interrupting you earlier; what were you going to say? You saw something?"

"Yes, that's why I know this is a dream."

"What was it?"

She shook her head.

"Come on, tell me."

"It was bad, Jeff. Something like that doesn't exist in reality."

"Okay then this is a dream, and because it is a dream you can tell me what your imagination conceived earlier when you saw it. Was it a man in black? With a mask?"

Her brow furrowed. "No. Why do you say that?"

"Never mind. Tell me, what was it?"

"It was an animal, I think. It was sort of far, so I'm not sure. It moved like an ape, using its arms as it went. It was olive green, hairless. I think it was coming from me; it was the first thing I saw when I woke up. It was running away from me."

I hummed meditatively. "You think it brought you here?"

"It wasn't very big." She shrugged. "Would have had to be strong."

"A green hairless ape," I mused, then chuckled, which offended my new friend.

"That amuses you, does it? Well I'm happy for you."

"No, it's just... well I don't know what else to do but laugh at this situation. It's a nightmare, I think we can both agree, but I don't know what else to do but laugh at it all. The more I think about it, the more I'm leaning toward dream as well. I'd guess that you didn't save that dress from your childhood only to wear decades later upon your abduction."

"Decades? Am I that old?"

"Don't you know how—" I guess she wouldn't know how old she is, being that she couldn't even recall her name. I didn't know my own age until I began recollecting the past recently. Emmy is eighteen and I'm sixteen years her senior, putting me at thirty four. "I guess you don't. No you're not old, I shouldn't have said decades. You're probably younger than me. I'm thirty-four, I think. Want to hear something strange? I have no idea what I look like. None whatsoever. I wish I had a mirror."

She cracked a grin. "Me too."

"I can tell you this: you're very pretty."

"You ain't so bad yourself." She sighed and scanned our environment. "What should we do?"

"No clue. What direction was that thing headed in?"

She pointed.

"Well I'm under the impression that an animal in this heat wouldn't stray too far from water, so if we can find where it went maybe we'll find something to drink. And if nothing else, if we find it and it's dead, we can still have a drink." Under my breath I muttered, "Even if it's not yet dead."

She looked sharply at me. "I couldn't do that."

"I think you could if you'd die otherwise. I know I sure would. Let's get a move on.

prompt: What is the most complex system in the human body, and how does it work?
response_a:
The most complex system in the human body is widely debated among scientists and medical professionals, as different systems have unique intricacies and interdependencies. However, many experts argue that the nervous system is the most complex due to its extensive network of cells, organs, and processes that enable us to think, feel, move, and interact with our environment.

The nervous system is composed of two main parts: the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord, while the PNS encompasses all the nerves that branch out from the CNS to other parts of the body.

The brain, the control center of the nervous system, is made up of billions of neurons, or nerve cells, that communicate with each other through electrical and chemical signals. Different regions of the brain perform specific functions, such as processing sensory information, regulating bodily functions, and generating movement.

Neurons are specialized cells that transmit information through long, thin extensions called axons and dendrites. Axons carry electrical impulses away from the cell body, while dendrites receive impulses from neighboring neurons. Synapses, the junctions between neurons, allow for communication between cells and the release of neurotransmitters, which are chemicals that facilitate signaling between neurons.

The nervous system also relies on support cells called glia, which provide structural and nutritional support to neurons and help regulate neural activity. There are several types of glial cells, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia, each with their own unique roles in maintaining neural health and function.

Overall, the complex interactions between neurons, glial cells, and neurotransmitters allow for the coordinated and dynamic functioning of the nervous system. However, this complexity can also make the nervous system susceptible to disorders and diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and epilepsy, which affect neural structure, function, and connectivity.
response_b:
The most complex system in the human body is widely debated, as different systems have varying levels of complexity based on their functions. However, one system that is often considered to be particularly intricate is the nervous system.

The nervous system is responsible for controlling and coordinating all of the body's activities, from regulating heart rate and breathing to processing sensory information and generating movement. It is composed of two main parts: the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord, while the PNS includes all of the nerves that branch out from the CNS to connect with various organs and tissues throughout the body. The neurons, or nerve cells, that make up these systems communicate with each other through electrical and chemical signals known as action potentials and synaptic transmissions, respectively.

One of the key features of the nervous system that contributes to its complexity is the presence of neural networks, which are interconnected groups of neurons that process information and perform specific functions. These networks can range from simple reflex circuits that trigger rapid responses to more complex structures like the cerebellum, which plays a critical role in motor control and learning.

Another factor that adds to the complexity of the nervous system is the existence of multiple neurotransmitter systems, which use different chemicals to transmit signals between neurons. Some of these systems, such as dopamine and serotonin, are involved in mood regulation and cognition, while others, like acetylcholine and glutamate, play roles in learning, memory, and attention.

Overall, the nervous system's complexity stems from its ability to process vast amounts of information simultaneously and coordinate responses to internal and external stimuli in real time. Its intricate architecture and diverse functions allow us to navigate our environments, learn new skills, and adapt to changing circumstances, making it a truly remarkable system deserving of continued study and exploration.

Random sequential adsorption (RSA) refers to a process where particles are randomly introduced in a system, and if they do not overlap any previously adsorbed particle, they adsorb and remain fixed for the rest of the process. RSA can be carried out in computer simulation, in a mathematical analysis, or in experiments. It was first studied by one-dimensional models: the attachment of pendant groups in a polymer chain by Paul Flory, and the car-parking problem by Alfréd Rényi. Other early works include those of Benjamin Widom. In two and higher dimensions many systems have been studied by computer simulation, including in 2d, disks, randomly oriented squares and rectangles, aligned squares and rectangles, various other shapes, etc.

An important result is the maximum surface coverage, called the saturation coverage or the packing fraction. On this page we list that coverage for many systems.

The blocking process has been studied in detail in terms of the random sequential adsorption (RSA) model. The simplest RSA model related to deposition of spherical particles considers irreversible adsorption of circular disks. One disk after another is placed randomly at a surface. prompt: Explain the difference between deism and theism. Make sure to include at least 4 key characteristics of each.
response_a:
Deism and theism are two distinct philosophical and religious beliefs that share some similarities but also have significant differences. While both views acknowledge the existence of a divine being, they differ in their understanding of God's nature, role, and relationship with the world. Here are four key characteristics that distinguish deism from theism:

Deism:

1. God is seen as an impersonal and distant creator: Deists believe that God created the universe and set it in motion, but then withdrew from it and no longer interacts with the world. They view God as an all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-perfect being who is transcendent, meaning He is separate and distinct from His creation.

2. Revelation is not necessary: Deists reject the idea of supernatural revelations or miracles, believing that God has revealed everything necessary for us to know about Him through reason and observation of the natural world.

3. Morality is based on reason: Since there is no ongoing communication between humans and God, deists argue that moral values must be derived from reason and logic rather than divine commandments.

4. Religious practice is minimal: Because deists do not see God as involved in day-to-day affairs, they do not place great importance on religious rituals, ceremonies, or institutions.

Theism:

1. God is personal and involved: Theistic religions like Judaism, Christianity, and Islam assert that God is an active and engaged creator who continues to interact with His creation. Unlike deists, theists believe that God reveals Himself to humanity through various means, including Scripture, prophecy, and miraculous events.

2. Revelation is necessary: Theists accept that God has communicated with humanity throughout history, providing guidance and instruction through sacred texts, teachings, and experiences.

3. Morality is grounded in God: Theistic religions emphasize that morality is rooted in God's character and commands, which are revealed through Scripture and other forms of divine communication.

4. Religious practice is essential: Theists regard religious worship, prayer, and community as integral components of their faith, serving as a way to deepen their connection with God and one another.

In summary, while both deism and theism acknowledge the existence of a divine being, deism emphasizes God
response_b:
Deism and theism are two philosophical and religious concepts that share some similarities but differ in significant ways. Here are four key characteristics that distinguish deism from theism:

1. Concept of God: The primary distinction between deism and theism lies in their views on the nature of God. Deists believe in a distant, impersonal, and watchmaker-like God who created the universe and then withdrew from it. They reject the idea of God's intervention in human affairs or involvement in daily events. In contrast, theists hold that God is an active and personal being who continues to interact with the world and its inhabitants.

2. Revelation: Another crucial difference between deism and theism is their stance on divine revelation. Deists argue that God revealed himself through nature and reason alone, and they reject the notion that God communicates through scripture, prophets, or miracles. Theists, on the other hand, believe that God has revealed his will and character through various means, including the Bible, the Quran, and other sacred texts.

3. Morality: Deists and theists also have different approaches to morality. Deists believe that moral values are innate and universal, based on reason and intuition rather than divine commandments. They contend that people can discern right and wrong without any reference to religion or divine guidance. Theists, however, maintain that morality is grounded in God's laws, which are revealed in scripture and reinforced by divine authority.

4. Salvation: Finally, deists and theists have divergent views on salvation. Deists reject the concept of original sin and affirm that humans are inherently good. They believe that individuals are responsible for their own salvation through their moral choices and rational reflection. Theists, in contrast, assert that humans are born with a sinful nature and require redemption through faith in God and acceptance of Jesus Christ as savior.

In summary, while both deism and theism acknowledge the existence of a divine being, deism emphasizes reason, natural law, and a distant creator, whereas theism stresses divine intervention, divine revelation, moral absolutes, and redemption through faith in God.

By Louise Swinn

5 October 2018 — 12:15am

The Helpline

The Helpline. By Katherine Collette.

Katherine Collette

Text has a knack of publishing debut novels with oddball protagonists. Reminiscent of the characters brought to life in Toni Jordan's Addition and Graeme Simsion's The Rosie Project, Katherine Collette's Germaine is a bit of a loner, particularly good with numbers, statistics and Sudoku, and a little bit socially awkward. Unlike Gail Honeyman's Eleanor Oliphant, traumatic events have not made her this way. She is a bit of an eccentric in the way that some people are; she finds social interaction difficult, and she has a deep respect for order and for rules, and does not appreciate when people flaunt them.

The title refers to the local council's senior citizen's helpline, the new workplace of our unlikely hero. The enormous success of The Office reflects the vast number of people who can relate to the cringeworthy aspects of working in such an environment. People who start off as complete strangers are forced to spend great swathes of time in close proximity. prompt: What are some of the health benefits of eating beets? Can they help with blood pressure or cancer prevention?

Yes, beets are packed with several health benefits, and studies have shown that consuming beets can indeed help with blood pressure and may have potential for cancer prevention. Here are some of the key health benefits of eating beets:

1. Lowers Blood Pressure: Beets contain nitrates, which are converted into nitric oxide in the body. Nitric oxide helps to relax and widen blood vessels, leading to a decrease in blood pressure. A study published in the American Journal of Hypertension found that drinking beet juice significantly lowered systolic blood pressure in people with hypertension.

2. Anti-Inflammatory Properties: Beets contain betaine, a compound that has anti-inflammatory properties. Chronic inflammation is linked to several diseases, including heart disease, diabetes, and cancer.

3. Rich in Nutrients: Beets are a good source of fiber, folate, manganese, potassium, and vitamin C. They also contain antioxidants like beta-cyanine and anthocyanins, which have been linked to a reduced risk of cancer.

4. May Help Prevent Cancer: Some studies suggest that compounds found in beets, such as betalains and pigenols, may have cancer-fighting properties. One study found that consuming beetroot extract led to a significant reduction in the growth of breast cancer cells.

5. Boosts Athletic Performance: The nitrates in beets have also been shown to improve athletic performance by increasing stamina and endurance during exercise. This is thought to be due to the improved oxygen delivery to muscles.

Overall, incorporating beets into your diet can provide many health benefits, from lowering blood pressure and boosting athletic performance to preventing chronic diseases like cancer.

prompt: What are some common types of tenements in London, United Kingdom? I want a list of five types using letters to indicate items (A., B., etc.).
response_a:
1. A. Type - This type of tenement is typically multi-storey and terraced, with each floor housing multiple families. The buildings are narrow and closely packed, often lacking natural light and ventilation. They were commonly built in the mid-19th century as a result of population growth and urbanization.

2. B. Type - These tenements are larger, more spacious buildings that house several flats or apartments per floor. They may also have communal facilities such as lifts, laundry rooms, and gardens. They became popular in the late 19th century as the demand for better living conditions increased.

3. C. Type - Also known as 'back-to-backs', these tenements are characterised by their layout, where two houses share a party wall at the back. Each house has its own entrance but shares a yard or alleyway. They were prevalent in working-class areas during the 19th century due to their affordability and ease of construction.

4. D. Type - These tenements feature a mix of commercial and residential spaces on the ground floor, with living quarters above. They were common in busy urban areas where shops and businesses could thrive alongside housing.

5. E. Type - Known as 'slum clearance' tenements, they replaced dilapidated and overcrowded buildings in impoverished areas. They were designed to provide better living conditions and social amenities, such as playgrounds and community centres. They emerged in the early 20th century as part of urban renewal initiatives.
response_b:
1. A-type tenements: These are multi-storey buildings with shared facilities like toilets and bathrooms on each floor. The flats within the building are typically small and basic, with little or no natural light or ventilation.

2. B-type tenements: Also known as "back-to-backs," these buildings have two or more houses built back-to-back, sharing a party wall. Each house has its own front door but no access to outside space other than a shared yard at the rear.

3. C-type tenements: Similar to A-type tenements, but with larger flats that may include separate kitchens and living rooms. Shared facilities like toilets and bathrooms are still located on each floor.

4. D-type tenements: These are large, imposing buildings with multiple storeys and many flats. They often have a central courtyard or garden, but flats may still be cramped and lack amenities like running water.

5. E-type tenements: The most modern type, E-type tenements offer self-contained flats with their own kitchens, bathrooms, and living spaces. While they may still be compact, they provide a higher standard of living than earlier types of tenements.

prompt: What is the difference between a fetus and an infant, and when does the fetus become an infant?
response_a:
A fetus refers to an unborn baby who is still developing inside its mother's womb. This stage typically lasts from conception until birth, which can be around 38-42 weeks (or nine months) for a full-term pregnancy. The fetal stage is characterized by rapid growth and development of essential organs and systems such as the brain, heart, lungs, and bones.

An infant, on the other hand, is a newborn baby who has been born and is now outside the womb. Infants continue to develop and grow after birth, but at a slower pace than during the fetal stage. The first few months of life are crucial for infants as they learn to adapt to their new environment, refine their senses, and develop important motor skills.

In summary, the main difference between a fetus and an infant is that a fetus is still developing inside the mother's womb, while an infant has already been born and is continuing to develop outside the womb. The transition from fetus to infant occurs at birth.
response_b:
A fetus is a developing organism during the later stages of pregnancy (from around week 8 until birth). It is enclosed in the mother's uterus and receives nutrients and oxygen through the placenta. The fetus cannot survive outside the womb as it is not fully developed to breathe, regulate body temperature, or maintain its own blood sugar levels.

An infant, on the other hand, is a newborn baby who has been born and is now outside the womb. Infants continue to develop and grow after birth, but they are now able to breathe, maintain their own body temperature, and receive nutrition from sources other than the placenta.

The transition from fetus to infant occurs at birth, which marks the end of the prenatal period and the beginning of extrauterine life for the baby.

Reference:
<start of reference>
Long charging times and a lack of public chargers are keeping people from buying electric cars. 
Some startups are convinced that EV charging needs a fundamental overhaul. 
Battery swapping and wireless EV charging could someday make owning an EV way more convenient. 
The thought of charging is scaring away potential electric car buyers. If everybody is expected to shun dirty fuels sooner rather than later, that needs to change.  
Sure, automakers can tackle the frustratingly long duration of charging stops by engineering cars that recharge more quickly and drive farther between fill-ups. Charging providers can put anxious drivers at ease by blanketing the country with a greater number of more reliable stations. And that's all happening. 
But some startups are convinced the way we refuel EVs needs a complete overhaul. 
When a battery dies, swap it
San Francisco-based Ample's pitch is simple: Instead of spending precious time waiting around to refill the same battery over and over, why not simply change it out for a fresh pack and be on your way? 
Ample's drive-through battery-swapping stations, roughly the size of a few parking spaces, are where the magic happens. After a driver pulls into a stall, their vehicle is lifted up and machinery below springs into action, autonomously plucking out the depleted pack and replacing it with a fully charged one in minutes. That's a game-changing improvement over typical fast-charging stations, where getting a solid charge could take 30 minutes to an hour or more. 
The firm is still in its very early days, but its tech is already in the hands of some Uber drivers in California thanks to a deal with the ride-hailing giant. Ample plans to focus on taxi, delivery, and car-rental fleets before turning its attention to regular consumers. 
You won't be able to pull up to an Ample station in just any EV — it'll need to be outfitted with the startup's modular, removable battery packs. The company plans to accomplish that through partnerships with automakers. 
Given our currently limited infrastructure and technology, EVs work best for people who don't drive very far in a day and can charge at home. Quick, convenient, and cheap battery swapping will be key for getting everyone else on board, John de Souza, Ample's cofounder and president, told Insider. 
"If you don't have the luxury of having a parking garage overnight, it starts falling apart," he said, referring to EV ownership. "Or if you drive a lot of miles, it falls apart."
Ample offers more than just speedy pit stops, de Souza said. Under the company's model, customers will buy a battery-less vehicle and then pay a battery subscription, potentially slashing the upfront cost of going electric. Battery swapping should extend vehicle longevity by cutting down on fast-charging sessions, which accelerate battery wear, and by letting owners keep up with the latest advances in battery chemistry, de Souza said. 
Chinese startup Nio has sold cars with swappable batteries for years while building out the infrastructure to support them — first in its homeland and now in Europe. Stateside, widespread battery swapping still looks a long way off, but it's gaining momentum. US EV startup Fisker recently announced plans to offer Ample's tech in its Ocean SUV starting in 2024. 
Electric cars, meet electric roads
For Israel's Electreon, the path toward an EV future is paved with roads that wirelessly recharge vehicles while they're moving.
The tech may sound like something straight out of science fiction, but it's real. Electreon's initial projects mainly bring wireless charging to public buses — vehicles with predictable routes and depots ripe for reinvention. But it's not stopping there. 
Oren Ezer, Electreon's cofounder and CEO, told Insider that wireless charging could solve the biggest challenges stunting the EV revolution: insufficient charging infrastructure, limited driving range, and a reliance on large, expensive batteries. In a world where electrified bus stops, parking spots, and streets charge vehicles all the time, those sticking points recede into the rearview. That's the long-term vision, anyway. 
To demonstrate the transformative potential of so-called "dynamic wireless charging," Electreon in May set out to drive a Toyota RAV4 Prime — a plug-in hybrid with just 42 miles of electric-only range — for 100 hours straight without plugging in or using any gas. 
On a test track with its copper charging coils embedded in the asphalt, Electreon and a team of 55 drivers covered 1,207 miles, a feat that would be unthinkable in a typical EV. (The cream of today's electric crop can travel 300-500 miles before they need to stop and recharge.)
The SUV, specially outfitted to receive energy wirelessly, looped the track at around 20-30 mph, Ezer said. He added that even at highway speeds, Electreon's roads can keep a vehicle's battery topped up indefinitely. 
Before you shudder at the prospect of endless, invasive construction if this tech takes off, consider this: Electreon says it can lay 1 mile of road in a night. It doesn't need to rip up an entire street, Ezer said, just dig a trench about three inches deep. 
Despite the billions pouring into conventional charging infrastructure, Ezer thinks his technology will win out someday. One positive sign: In March, Electreon announced an R&D partnership with Toyota.

prompt: What are some ways to build self-confidence, especially during a job interview?
response_a:
1. Preparation: One of the most effective ways to build self-confidence during a job interview is to prepare thoroughly. Research the company and the position you're applying for, review common interview questions, and practice answering them out loud. This will help you feel more confident and prepared when the actual interview takes place.

2. Positive Self-Talk: Negative thoughts can be detrimental to your confidence level. Instead, try to replace negative self-talk with positive affirmations. Remind yourself of your strengths, accomplishments, and why you would be an asset to the company.

3. Practice Active Listening: Listen carefully to the interviewer's questions and respond thoughtfully. Make eye contact, nod your head, and show that you're engaged in the conversation. This will demonstrate your confidence and interest in the position.

4. Body Language: Your body language can communicate confidence or nervousness. Sit up straight, make eye contact, and smile. Avoid fidgeting, slouching, or crossing your arms as these can convey defensiveness or discomfort.

5. Be Authentic: Don't try to be someone you're not during the interview. Be true to yourself and your experiences. Speak confidently about your skills and accomplishments, but also acknowledge areas where you may need improvement.

6. Ask Questions: Prepare a list of thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer. This shows that you've done your research and are genuinely interested in the company and the position. It also provides an opportunity to learn more about the role and the company culture.

7. Follow Up: After the interview, send a thank-you note or email to the interviewer. This demonstrates your appreciation for their time and reiterates your interest in the position. It's also a great opportunity to remind the interviewer of your qualifications and why you'd be a good fit for the company.

Remember, confidence is contagious. If you project confidence and enthusiasm during the interview, it can go a long way in making a positive impression on the interviewer. Good luck!
response_b:
1. Preparation: One of the best ways to build self-confidence during a job interview is to prepare thoroughly. This includes researching the company, practicing common interview questions, and reviewing your resume and qualifications. The more prepared you are, the more confident you will feel.

2. Positive Self-Talk: Try to replace negative thoughts with positive affirmations. Instead of thinking "I'm not good enough for this job," say "I am qualified and have valuable skills to offer." Speak kindly to yourself and focus on your strengths.

5. Visualization: Before the interview, take some time to visualize yourself succeeding. Picture yourself answering questions confidently and making a strong impression. This can help boost your confidence and reduce anxiety.

6. Dress Appropriately: Wear clothing that makes you feel confident and comfortable. Choose an outfit that fits well and flatters your body type. Dress appropriately for the company culture and position you are applying for.

7. Focus on Listening: During the interview, make an effort to listen carefully to the interviewer's questions. This will help you provide thoughtful and insightful answers, which will further boost your confidence.

8. Ask Questions: Asking questions shows that you are interested in the company and the position. It also gives you a chance to learn more about the role and the company culture. This can help you feel more informed and confident during the interview.

9. Follow Up: After the interview, send a thank-you note or email to the interviewer. This shows that you appreciate their time and are grateful for the opportunity. It also allows you to reiterate your interest in the position and further reinforce your confidence.

Remember, building self-confidence takes practice and persistence. Keep working on these strategies, and over time, you will become more confident and successful in your job interviews.

Many Americans face "hunger crisis" as food insecurity rises
BY AIMEE PICCHI
MAY 31, 2023 / 8:14 AM / MONEYWATCH

Anti-hunger advocates say the U.S. is facing an "unprecedented" rise in food insecurity amid persistently high inflation in the grocery aisle and cuts to the food-stamp program earlier this year.

The rise in food insecurity — lacking enough food to live a healthy, active life — comes as the nation has ended the pandemic emergency and the economy, by many measures, continues to be strong. The unemployment rate is near a 50-year low, while wages have been rising for many workers. 

But those figures hide a stark reality that's affecting a growing share of U.S. households, ranging from young families to older Americans. Although jobs are plentiful, many employees don't earn enough to cover the surging cost of living, pushing some to make tradeoffs like skipping meals. 

And cuts to the food-stamp program earlier this year reduced benefits at a time when groceries are 20% costlier than two years ago. That caused food insecurity to jump to "unprecedented levels" in May among food-stamp recipients, according to a new survey from Propel, which makes an app for beneficiaries to check balances for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, (formerly known as food stamps).

About 44% of respondents reported skipping meals in the last month, a 7% increase and a record high, Propel noted. Those findings were echoed in a new study from the Greater Boston Food Bank, which found that some local families are making desperate choices, such as watering down baby formula or other food. 

"When I see one in three households with children reporting that their children were hungry, or they skipped a meal, that shouldn't happen," said Catherine D'Amato, CEO of the Greater Boston Food Bank, told CBS MoneyWatch. "This shows this is a hunger crisis that is persisting in Massachusetts."

D'Amato said that current rates of food insecurity are the highest she has ever seen in her career. Her group's study, released Tuesday, found that 33% of Massachusetts households were food insecure in 2022, while 36% of those with children didn't have enough food last year. 

The research jibes with findings from the U.S. Census, which for three years has asked households about their food consumption. The number of Americans who say they sometimes don't have enough to eat has jumped 23% — from 15.8 million prior to the pandemic to 19.2 million in the most recent survey, taken in late April and early May. 

New food-stamp work requirements
The rise in food insecurity comes as the debt ceiling deal, struck between the White House and Republican lawmakers, would add more work requirements to SNAP. That could create more hardship for a greater number of struggling Americans, D'Amato predicted. 

"The SNAP cuts and the work requirements are really going to be harmful," she added. "We don't know to what extent until we see the final debt ceiling agreements and how it gets rolled out."

SNAP already includes work requirements for low-income people ages 18 to 49 who are able-bodied and without dependents. Under the deal, that age limit would be raised to 54 years old, which could hurt older workers without a stable income and potentially put them at risk of losing food aid, experts said. 

However, the deal would temporarily eliminate SNAP work requirements for veterans and those experiencing homelessness, regardless of age. Those exceptions, as well as the higher age limit for work requirements, would expire in 2030.

About 700,000 people between the ages of 50 to 54 would be impacted by the new work requirements, according to the Wall Street Journal. But by eliminating work requirements for veterans and homeless people, about 78,000 people would gain benefits each month, the Congressional Budget Office said in a Tuesday report. 

Together, the changes to SNAP would boost government spending by $2.1 billion over the next decade, the CBO estimated.

Tradeoffs: Groceries or rent?
In the meantime, low-income Americans are increasingly making tradeoffs and experiencing broader hardships as they cope with the rising cost of groceries and cuts to their food aid, research shows. Eviction rates for food-stamp recipients soared by 40% from April to May, while 11% of respondents had their utilities cut off in the last month, a 24% jump from the prior month, Propel found.

A majority of households in Massachusetts who experienced food insecurity last year reporting having to decide between paying for food or covering rent, utilities and other costs, the Greater Boston Food Bank found. And almost one-third said they had watered down food or infant formula to make ends meet, while 85% said they bought the cheapest food available. 

"You hear this in health care, that 'I skipped my medication for a day'," but now people are making these same choices with food, D'Amato said. "It's shocking, though not surprising, that families are in a situation where they have to make tradeoffs."

prompt: What is the origin of the obi in Japan? Why did it become popular?
response_a:
The obi, which is a wide sash worn around the waist to fasten a kimono in Japan, has a rich history dating back several centuries. The exact origin of the obi is unclear, but it is believed to have evolved from the traditional Japanese belt known as a kuzakamaki, which was used to secure the kimono during the Heian period (794-1185).

During the Edo period (1603-1868), the obi became more elaborate and decorative due to the influence of the ruling samurai class. The samurai would wear a wide obi with intricate designs as a symbol of their wealth and status. This trend spread to the general population, and soon the obi became an essential part of the traditional Japanese wardrobe.

One reason for the popularity of the obi is its versatility. It can be tied in various ways to create different styles and looks, ranging from simple and understated to extravagant and ornate. Additionally, the obi provides a blank canvas for artistic expression through its patterns and colors, making it a cherished item for both fashion enthusiasts and collectors alike.

Another factor contributing to the enduring popularity of the obi is its cultural significance. In Japanese culture, the kimono and obi represent a connection to tradition and heritage. Wearing them allows individuals to pay homage to their roots and celebrate their identity. As such, the obi remains a staple of Japanese fashion and continues to inspire new trends and innovations today.

In summary, the origin of the obi in Japan can be traced back to the traditional Japanese belt, but it evolved into a more elaborate and decorative accessory during the Edo period due to the influence of the samurai class. Its popularity is attributed to its versatility, artistic expression, and cultural significance, all of which continue to make it an important part of Japanese fashion and culture today.

The obi became not just a functional piece but also a symbol of beauty, elegance, and femininity.

In summary, the obi's origins can be traced back to the Heian period, where it served a practical purpose. However, during the Edo period, it transformed into a status symbol and a fashion statement due to sumptuary laws and the influence of ukiyo-e art. The history of rock music has been volatile and unpredictable as the genre has constantly redefined and reinvented itself since its emergence in the late 1940s. Not surprisingly, then, it can be difficult to apply a straightforward definition to such a restless musical format.

But while people might quibble over specifics, rock music can generally be described as hard-edged music performed with electric guitars, bass, and drums and usually accompanied by lyrics sung by a vocalist. That sounds simple enough, but a closer look at the evolution of rock suggests how different styles and influences have shaped its development over the years.

Rock’s origins can be traced to the late 1940s, when the popular styles of the day, country music and blues, morphed into a new sound aided by electric guitars and a steady drumbeat. Pioneering rock artists of the 1950s such as Chuck Berry leaned heavily on classic blues structures while demonstrating a flair as natural-born entertainers. In contrast to the safe pop music of the era, rock’s aggressive attack suggested a sexual freedom that was shocking during that conservative age.

By the early '60s, Berry’s followers, most notably the Rolling Stones, expanded rock’s scope by transitioning from singles artists into musicians capable of producing cohesive albums of songs. Embracing sex and youthful rebellion in their music, the Stones courted controversy but also elevated rock to new cultural heights.

As rock music became the dominant form of popular music, new bands built on their predecessors’ strengths while branching out into new sonic territory. Led Zeppelin gave rock a darker, heavier tone, becoming one of the '70s’ most popular bands and helping to kick-start a new genre known as hard rock or heavy metal.

Around the same time, Pink Floyd added psychedelic elements and complex arrangements, creating concept albums tied together by a single theme and meant to be absorbed in a single sitting. Albums such as "Dark Side of the Moon" were credited with spawning the progressive rock movement.

In the late '70s, in response to what they perceived as pretentious “hippie” bands such as Pink Floyd, groups including the Sex Pistols and the Clash simplified rock to its core ingredients: loud guitars, rude attitude, and enraged singing. Punk was born.

While all three movements enjoyed different degrees of mainstream acceptance, a fourth, less-recognized style was beginning to take shape. Spotlighting atonal noise and unconventional rock instruments such as drum machines, groups such as Pere Ubu became the pioneers of industrial rock, an abrasive sub-genre that didn’t enjoy widespread popularity but inspired future rock bands.

As the '80s began, mainstream rock was losing commercial steam, its sound growing stale. In such a creatively stagnant environment, subgenres started to assert their dominance.

Inspired by punk’s outsider status and industrial’s eclectic instrumentation, keyboard-driven English bands such as Depeche Mode demonstrated a more introverted songwriting style, creating post-punk, also described as new wave.

Meanwhile, American groups including R.E.M. toyed with post-punk elements, balancing introspective lyrics with traditional rock-band arrangements. These bands were dubbed college rock because of their popularity on college radio stations.

By the end of the '80s, college rock had become such a lucrative alternative to mainstream rock that it received a new moniker: alternative rock. It was also called indie rock because the bands were often signed to small, independently owned labels.

Alternative rock cemented its cultural standing when the music magazine Billboard created a new chart in 1988 for alternative rock, which the publication classified as modern rock. For most music fans, terms such as modern rock, alternative, and indie are synonymous ways of describing this popular sub-genre.

Normal Forms

Normalization is achieved through a set of rules called Normal Forms (NF). There are several levels of NF, but we'll focus on three primary ones: First Normal Form (1NF), Second Normal Form (2NF), and Third Normal Form (3NF). Here's a brief overview of each:

First Normal Form (1NF): A table is said to be in 1NF when all its attributes are atomic or scalar, meaning they cannot be further divided into smaller parts. In other words, each cell in the table contains only one value.

Second Normal Form (2NF): A table is in 2NF if it's in 1NF and every non-key attribute is functionally dependent on the primary key. This means that no partial dependency exists between any non-key attribute and the primary key.

Third Normal Form (3NF): A table is in 3NF if it's in 2NF and there's no transitive dependency between non-key attributes. This means that no attribute is dependent on another non-key attribute, except through the primary key.

Reduced Data Redundancy: By applying normalization techniques, we can eliminate redundant data from our tables. If we have multiple orders for the same customer, we end up storing their name and address multiple times, leading to data redundancy. By normalizing this table, we can create a separate customer table with the customer's name and address, and then reference it in the order table using a foreign key. This approach eliminates redundant data and reduces storage requirements.

prompt: What are some examples of might in the English language? Why is might used instead of can in some sentences?
response_a:
Might is a modal auxiliary verb in the English language that expresses possibility, probability, or potentiality. Some examples of might in sentences are:

1. If I had more time, I might finish the project today. (Here, might is used to indicate a possibility.)

2. She might be at the party tonight. (Here, might is used to indicate a probability based on available information.)

3. In ancient times, people might have believed that the sun moved around the earth. (Here, might is used to indicate a potentiality or hypothetical situation.)

Might is often used instead of can in some sentences because it adds a sense of uncertainty, doubt, or politeness. For example:

1. You might want to consider this option. (This sentence suggests that there is a possibility or probability that the person may want to consider the option.)

2. The decision might take some time. (This sentence indicates that the decision is not certain and may take longer than expected.)

3. Might I ask you a question? (This sentence is more polite than "Can I ask you a question?" and indicates that the speaker is unsure whether the person will agree to answer their question.)

In summary, might is a versatile word in the English language that adds nuance and shades of meaning to sentences by expressing possibility, probability, or potentiality. Its use instead of can adds a degree of uncertainty, doubt, or politeness.
response_b:
Might is a modal auxiliary verb in English that indicates possibility, probability, or uncertainty in the past, present, or future. Some examples of might in the English language are:

1. Past tense: "She might have gone to the store yesterday." This sentence expresses a possibility or uncertainty about the past.

2. Present tense: "The weather might change later today." This sentence suggests a potential future event with some degree of likelihood.

3. Future tense: "By this time next year, he might have graduated from college." Here, might indicates a lower level of certainty compared to will or shall for future events.

Might is often used instead of can in some sentences to convey a lower degree of certainty, possibility, or politeness. For example:

1. "I might be able to help you with that" instead of "I can help you with that".

2. "You might want to consider this option" instead of "You should consider this option".

In these cases, using might instead of can adds a level of uncertainty or politeness to the statement, making it less forceful and more tentative. It also allows for a greater degree of flexibility and adaptability in communication, as it leaves room for alternative outcomes or interpretations.

prompt: What are the different types of iron ore, and what metals can they be used to produce?
response_a:
There are several types of iron ores, each with varying levels of iron content:

1. Hematite (Fe2O3): This is the most common type of iron ore, accounting for about 70% of all iron ores mined. It contains approximately 67-74% iron and can be used to produce high-grade iron products like steel.

2. Magnetite (Fe3O4): This type of iron ore is magnetic and contains approximately 72% iron. It is commonly found in rocks and sedimentary deposits. Magnetite is often used to make iron in electric arc furnaces.

3. Limonite (FeO(OH)): This is a brownish-yellow iron ore that contains around 50-60% iron. It is commonly found in sedimentary deposits and is often mixed with other iron ores to increase their iron content.

4. Siderite (FeCO3): This is an uncommon type of iron ore that contains approximately 48% iron. It is typically found in sedimentary deposits and is often converted into another form of iron ore before being processed.

In addition to iron, these iron ores can also contain impurities such as sulfur, phosphorus, and silica, which must be removed during the processing and refining stages. Once purified, the iron can be used to produce a variety of metal products, including steel, pipes, construction materials, and appliances. Other metals that may be produced from iron ores include nickel, cobalt, and platinum group elements like platinum, palladium, and gold. However, these metals are typically found in much smaller quantities than iron.

2. Magnetite (Fe3O4): This ore has a much higher iron content than hematite, around 70%, but it also contains significant amounts of impurities such as silica and alumina. Magnetite is often upgraded using processing techniques before it can be used to make steel.

3. Limonite (FeO(OH)): This ore is lower in iron content than hematite and magnetite, typically containing around 30-40% iron. Limonite often occurs in sedimentary deposits and can be challenging to extract due to its soft consistency.

4. Siderite (FeCO3): This ore is less common than the others and contains significantly less iron, around 15-30%. It's often found in association with limestone deposits and is sometimes used as a source of iron in the steelmaking process.

Iron ores are primarily used to produce iron and steel products. Iron can be used to make a variety of products, including structural steel, reinforcing bars, nails, and screws. Steel, which is an alloy of iron and carbon, is used in many applications, from construction materials like beams and girders to automobile bodies and appliances. Other metals that can be produced from iron ores include nickel, cobalt, and vanadium, which may be present as impurities in some iron ores. However, these metals are typically extracted through more specialized mining and refining processes rather than directly from the iron ore itself.

prompt: What are some examples of space probes that have explored the planet Mars?
response_a:
Some notable space probes that have explored Mars include:

1. Viking 1 and Viking 2 (launched in 1975): These twin spacecraft successfully landed on Mars in 1976 and conducted extensive scientific studies, including searches for signs of life.

2. Pathfinder (launched in 1996): This mission included the successful landing of the Mars Rover, Sojourner, which was the first rover to operate on the Martian surface.

3. Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) (launched in 1996): This orbiter provided detailed maps of the Martian surface and atmosphere, as well as data on its geology and climate history.

4. Mars Odyssey (launched in 2001): This orbiter discovered evidence of water ice at the Martian poles and helped pave the way for future human missions by studying radiation levels.

5. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) (launched in 2005): This orbiter has provided high-resolution images of the Martian surface, including features such as canyons, craters, and volcanoes.

6. Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) Curiosity Rover (launched in 2011): This rover is still exploring Gale Crater and has made significant discoveries about the geology and potential habitability of Mars.

7. Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution (MAVEN) Orbiter (launched in 2013): This mission is focused on understanding the evolution of the Martian atmosphere and how it may have contributed to the loss of water over time.

These missions have greatly expanded our knowledge of Mars and helped us better understand its geology, climate, and potential for supporting life. Many more missions are currently under development or planned for the coming years, including NASA's Mars 2020 Rover and the European Space Agency's ExoMars Rover mission.
response_b:
1. Viking 1 and Viking 2 (launched in 1975): These were the first successful missions to land on Mars, with Viking 1 landing in July 1976 and Viking 2 following in September of the same year. Both probes operated for several years, transmitting data about the Martian atmosphere, surface features, and potential signs of life.

2. Pathfinder/Sojourner (launched in 1996): This mission was a major breakthrough in Mars exploration as it included a rover named Sojourner, which successfully navigated the Martian terrain in search of geological features. The Pathfinder probe also transmitted high-resolution images and weather data from the Martian surface.

3. Mars Global Surveyor (launched in 1996): This orbiter circled Mars for over eight years, providing detailed maps and photographs of the planet's geology and atmosphere. It also discovered evidence of ancient water flows on the Martian surface.

4. Mars Odyssey (launched in 2001): This probe became the first Mars mission to detect signs of past water activity on the planet's surface, using its gamma ray spectrometer to analyze the composition of Martian rocks and soil.

5. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (launched in 2005): This spacecraft has been instrumental in mapping the Martian surface and identifying potential landing sites for future manned missions. Its High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera has captured stunning images of the Red Planet.

6. Phoenix (launched in 2007): This robotic lander was designed to study the Martian polar regions in search of ice and other signs of past or present water activity. Phoenix successfully landed in May 2008 and operated until November of the same year.

7. Curiosity (launched in 2011): This rover is currently exploring Gale Crater on Mars, searching for evidence of past microbial life. It has already discovered organic compounds and evidence of an ancient lake bed, indicating that Mars may once have been habitable.

These are just a few examples of the many space probes that have explored Mars over the years. As technology continues to advance, we can expect even more exciting discoveries and missions
